p.x:
Last year, I bought a new phone. It was expensive, so I also bought phone insurance. I pay 99 baht every month. My brother laughed. "That's a waste of money!" he said.
Two months later, I dropped my phone in the river. I was very sad. But then I remembered my insurance. I filled in a form on the website and sent some documents, like my receipt. After two weeks, the company paid the money into my bank account, and I bought a new phone.
Now my brother has insurance too! He says the monthly payment is small, but it's good to feel safe all year.

Many people go on holiday without travel insurance because they think it's not necessary. But unexpected problems can happen to anyone. You might lose your bag, miss a flight or get sick abroad. Health insurance from your home country may not cover medical costs in other countries, and a hospital bill can be thousands of dollars.
Before you buy, get a quote from two or three companies. Compare the premium (the price you pay) and what is covered. Read the small print carefully! Some policies don't cover risky activities like scuba diving. Others won't reimburse you if you don't report a theft to the police.
If something goes wrong, contact your insurer quickly. As the policyholder, you'll need to fill in a form and send evidence, such as receipts. Sometimes an inspector will check the damage. If your claim is accepted, you'll get a payout. A good broker can help you find the right policy.
Other types of insurance are also important. Car insurance is required by law in Thailand, and many families insure their homes against fire and flooding. Remember to renew your policy before it expires; most are annual. Insurance won't stop a mishap from happening, but it can compensate you for the cost and give you peace of mind. It works like a safety net, alongside a personal emergency fund.

At its simplest, insurance is a way of sharing risk. Thousands of people pay a relatively small amount into a common fund, and those who suffer a loss are paid from it. Because only a few policyholders will make a claim in any given year, the system can protect everyone at a manageable cost.
Calculating that cost is the job of the actuary, a specialist who uses statistics to estimate how likely different events are. Insurance companies then decide which risks to underwrite and at what price. A young driver with a powerful car, for example, will usually pay more than an experienced driver with a small one, because the data show a higher probability of accidents.
Policies also include conditions designed to limit costs. The excess is the amount the policyholder must pay before the insurer contributes. An exclusion is an event the policy does not cover; many standard home policies, for instance, exclude earthquakes. Insurers may also refuse claims caused by negligence, such as leaving a door unlocked, or by an obvious hazard the owner failed to fix. After a major incident, a loss adjuster will investigate to decide how much should be paid.
Critics argue that the industry sometimes makes policies deliberately confusing. Supporters reply that insurance remains one of the most prudent financial decisions a family can make. Life insurance, in particular, ensures that dependants are protected if the main earner dies. As climate change makes catastrophic events more frequent, the question of who can afford protection, and who will be left without it, is becoming increasingly urgent. Sensible precautions, such as installing smoke alarms, can also reduce premiums.
